source_text: Καὶ τί δεῖ τοὺς ἄλλους ἀπαριθμεῖσθαι οὓς αἱ Ῥιπαὶ γεννῶσι, τὰ ὑπὲρ τῆς ἐνδοτάτω Σκυθίας ὄρη; Ὧν ἐστὶ καὶ ὁ Ῥοδανὸς μετὰ μυρίων ἄλλων ποταμῶν, καὶ αὐτῶν ναυσιπόρων, οἳ τοὺς ἑσπερίους Γαλάτας καὶ Κελτοὺς, καὶ τοὺς προσεχεῖς αὐτοῖς βαρβάρους παραμειψάμενοι, ἐπὶ τὸ ἑσπέριον πάντες εἰσχέονται πέλαγος. Ἄλλοι ἐκ τῆς μεσημβρίας ἄνωθεν διὰ τῆς Αἰθιοπίας, οἱ μὲν ἐπὶ τὴν πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἔρχονται θάλασσαν· οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ τὴν ἔξω τῆς πλεομένης ἀποκενοῦνται· ὅ τε Αἰγὼν καὶ ὁ Νύσης καὶ ὁ καλούμενος Χρεμέτης, καὶ πρός γε ἔτι ὁ Νεῖλος, ὃς οὐδὲ ποταμοῖς τὴν φύσιν ἔοικεν, ὅταν ἴσα θαλάσσῃ πελαγίζῃ τὴν Αἴγυπτον. Οὕτως ὁ τῆς καθ' ἡμᾶς οἰκουμένης τόπος ὕδατι περιείληπται, πελάγεσί τε ἀπλέτοις ἐνδεδεμένος καὶ μυρίοις ποταμοῖς ἀεννάοις κατάρρυτος, διὰ τὴν ἄρρητον σοφίαν τοῦ τὴν ἀντίπαλον τῷ πυρὶ φύσιν δυσεξανάλωτον εἶναι οἰκονομήσαντος. Ἔσται μέντοι ὅτε καὶ πάντα καταφρυ γήσεται τῷ πυρὶ, ὥς φησιν Ἡσαΐας ἐν οἷς πρὸς τὸν τῶν ὅλων Θεὸν διαλέγεται· Ὁ λέγων τῇ ἀβύσσῳ, ἐρημωθήσῃ, καὶ πάντας τοὺς ποταμούς σου ξηρανῶ. Ὥστε ἀπορρίψας τὴν μωρανθεῖσαν σοφίαν, κατάδεξαι μεθ' ἡμῶν τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς ἀληθείας, ἰδιωτικὸν μὲν τῷ λόγῳ, ἀδιάπτωτον δὲ κατὰ τὴν γνῶσιν. 3.7 Διὰ τοῦτο Γενηθήτω στερέωμα ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ ὕδατος, καὶ ἔστω διαχωρίζον ἀνὰ μέσον ὕδατος καὶ ὕδατος. Εἴρηται τί τὸ σημαινόμενον παρὰ τῇ Γραφῇ τὸ τοῦ στερεώματος ὄνομα. Ὅτι οὐχὶ τὴν ἀντίτυπον καὶ στερέμνιον φύσιν, τὴν ἔχουσαν βάρος καὶ ἀντέρεισιν, οὐ ταύτην λέγει στερέωμα. Ἢ οὕτω ἂν κυριώτερον ἡ γῆ τῆς τοιαύτης κλήσεως ἠξιώθη. Ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν φύσιν τῶν ὑπερκειμένων λεπτὴν οὖσαν καὶ ἀραιὰν καὶ οὐδεμιᾷ αἰσθήσει καταληπτὴν, στερέωμα τοῦτο ὠνόμασε, συγκρίσει τῶν λεπτοτάτων καὶ τῇ αἰσθήσει ἀκαταλήπτων. Καὶ νόει μοι τόπον τινὰ διακριτικὸν τοῦ ὑγροῦ· τὸ μὲν λεπτὸν καὶ διηθούμενον ἐπὶ τὰ ἄνω διιέντα, τὸ δὲ παχύτατον καὶ γεῶδες ἐναφιέντα τοῖς κάτω, ἵν' ἐξ ἀρχῆς μέχρι τέλους ἡ αὐτὴ εὐκρασία συντηρηθῇ, κατὰ μέρος τῆς ὑφαιρέσεως τῶν ὑγρῶν γινομένης. Σὺ δὲ τῷ μὲν πλήθει τοῦ ὕδατος ἀπιστεῖς, πρὸς δὲ τοῦ θερμοῦ τὸ πλῆθος οὐκ ἀποβλέπεις· ὃ κἂν ὀλίγον ᾖ τῷ μεγέθει, πολλῆς ἐστι διὰ τὴν δύναμιν ἀναλωτικὸν ὑγρασίας. Ἐφέλκεται μὲν γὰρ τὸ παρακείμενον ὑγρὸν, ὡς δηλοῖ ἡ σικύα· δαπανητικὸν δέ ἐστι τοῦ ἑλκυσθέντος κατὰ τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ λυχνιαίου πυρὸς, ὃ διὰ τῆς θρυαλλίδος τὴν παρακειμένην τροφὴν ἐπισπασάμενον, ταχέως διὰ τῆς μεταβολῆς ἀπῃθάλωσε. Τὸν δὲ αἰθέρα τίς ἀμφιβάλλει μὴ οὐχὶ πυρώδη εἶναι καὶ διακαῆ; ὃς εἰ μὴ τῷ ἀναγκαίῳ τοῦ ποιήσαντος αὐτὸν ὅρῳ κατείχετο, τί ἂν ἐκώλυσεν αὐτὸν πάντα φλογίζοντα καὶ καταπιμπρῶντα τὰ συνεχῆ, πᾶσαν ὁμοῦ τὴν ἐν τοῖς οὖσιν ἐξαναλῶσαι νοτίδα; Διὰ ταῦτα ὕδωρ ἀέριον, νεφουμένου τοῦ ἄνω τόπου ἐκ τῆς ἀναφορᾶς τῶν ἀτμῶν, οὓς ποταμοὶ, καὶ κρῆναι, καὶ τενάγη, καὶ λίμναι, καὶ πελάγη πάντα προΐενται, ὡς ἂν μὴ πάντα πυρακτῶν ὁ αἰθὴρ ἐπιλάβοι· ὅπου γε καὶ τὸν ἥλιον τοῦτον ὁρῶμεν, ὥρᾳ θέρους διάβροχον πολλάκις καὶ τεναγώδη χώραν ἐν βραχυτάτῃ χρόνου ῥοπῇ ἄνικμον παντελῶς καὶ ξηρὰν καταλιμπάνοντα.
thought_title: Rivers and the fiery heaven: why water abounds
orientation: Basil is still cataloguing the rivers of the world and now turns to explain why the earth is so abundantly watered, arguing that water tempers the fiery nature of the upper region.
pass_a_gloss: And why is it necessary to enumerate the others which the Rhipaean mountains generate, the mountains beyond innermost Scythia? Of these is also the Rhodanus with countless other rivers, themselves also navigable, which, having passed by the western Galatians and Celts and the barbarians adjacent to them, all pour into the western sea. Others from the south from above through Ethiopia, some come to the sea toward us; others empty into the sea outside the navigated one; the Aegon and the Nyses and the one called Chremetes, and in addition still the Nile, which does not even resemble rivers in nature, whenever it floods Egypt like a sea. Thus the region of our inhabited world is surrounded by water, bound by immense seas and watered by countless ever-flowing rivers, because of the ineffable wisdom of the one who arranged that the nature opposed to fire be hard to consume. There will be a time, however, when all things will be burned up by fire, as Isaiah says in the words in which he converses with the God of all: He who says to the deep, You shall be made desolate, and all your rivers I will dry up. Therefore, having cast away the wisdom that has become foolish, accept with us the teaching of the truth, unskilled in speech, but infallible in knowledge. 3.7 For this reason let a firmament come to be in the midst of the water, and let it be separating between water and water. It has been said what the meaning of the name of the firmament is in Scripture. That it is not the resistant and solid nature, the one having weight and resistance, not this does it call firmament. Or thus more properly would the earth have been deemed worthy of such a name. But because of the nature of the things lying above, being fine and loose and perceptible by no sense, it named this firmament, by comparison with the finest things and those imperceptible to sense. And understand for me some place separating the moist; the fine and filtered part passing through to the upper regions, the thickest and earthy part being discharged to the lower regions, so that from beginning to end the same good temperature may be preserved, the subtraction of the moist parts happening in due measure. But you distrust the abundance of water, yet you do not look at the abundance of the hot; which even if it is small in size, is capable of consuming much moisture because of its power. For it draws to itself the adjacent moisture, as the cupping instrument shows; and it is consuming of what has been drawn, according to the image of the lamp fire, which, having drawn up through the wick the adjacent fuel, quickly through the change turned it to ash. And who doubts that the ether is fiery and intensely hot? Which if it were not held by the necessary boundary of its maker, what would have prevented it, flaming and burning up all things continuous, from consuming all at once the moisture in existing things? For this reason aerial water, the upper region being clouded from the rising of vapors, which rivers and springs and marshes and lakes and seas all send forth, so that the ether, burning all things, might not seize everything; since indeed we see this sun, in the season of summer, often leaving a soaked and marshy land in the briefest moment of time completely without moisture and dry.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for the expanse separating waters above from waters below.
Basil explicitly denies that the firmament is a hard, weighty substance; the adjectives contrast with the fine, loose nature he attributes to it.
Refers to the balanced mixture of elements, especially moisture and heat, preserved in the cosmos.
Basil describes water in the upper region formed from vapors, which tempers the fiery ether.
Fixed glossary term for the deep water, here quoted from Isaiah.
Echoes Paul's language about worldly wisdom being made foolish; Basil contrasts it with the teaching of truth.

pass_b_english: And why should I list the rest of the rivers born from the Rhipaean mountains, the heights beyond the innermost part of Scythia? Among them is the Rhone, along with countless other rivers, themselves navigable, which pass by the western Gauls and Celts and the barbarians bordering them, and all pour into the western sea. Others come from the south, from above through Ethiopia: some flow toward our sea, while others empty into the sea beyond the one that is sailed. There are the Aegon, the Nyses, and the one called Chremetes, and besides these the Nile, whose nature is not even like that of rivers when it floods Egypt like a sea. So the region of our inhabited world is surrounded by water, bound by immense seas and watered by countless ever-flowing rivers, through the ineffable wisdom of the One who arranged that the nature opposed to fire should be hard to consume. Yet there will come a time when all things will be burned up by fire, as Isaiah says in the words he addresses to the God of all: 'He who says to the deep, You shall be made desolate, and I will dry up all your rivers' (Isaiah 44:27). Therefore cast away the wisdom that has become foolish, and accept with us the teaching of truth, plain in its speech but infallible in its knowledge.

For this reason: 'Let a firmament come into being in the midst of the water, and let it separate water from water' (Genesis 1:6). We have already said what the name 'firmament' means in Scripture. It does not mean a resistant and solid nature, one that has weight and offers resistance—Scripture does not call that a firmament. If it did, the earth would more properly have been given that name. But because the nature of the things above is fine and loose and not graspable by any sense, Scripture named it 'firmament' by comparison with the finest things that are imperceptible to the senses. And understand it as a place that separates the moist element: the fine and filtered part passes through to the upper regions, while the thickest and earthiest part is released below, so that from beginning to end the same good temperature may be preserved, as the moist elements are gradually drawn off in part. But you distrust the abundance of water, while you do not consider the abundance of heat—which, even if small in size, is capable of consuming a great deal of moisture because of its power. For it draws in the moisture that lies near it, as the cupping glass shows; and it consumes what it has drawn in, like the fire of a lamp, which draws up the fuel that lies near it through the wick and quickly turns it to ash through the change. And who doubts that the ether is fiery and burning hot? If it were not held back by the necessary limit set by its Maker, what would prevent it from setting everything ablaze and burning up all that is near it, consuming at once all the moisture in all things? For this reason there is aerial water, as the upper region becomes cloudy from the rising of vapors that rivers and springs and marshes and lakes and seas all send forth, so that the ether may not seize everything and set it on fire. Indeed, we see this very sun, in the summer season, often leaving a soaked and marshy land completely dry and parched in the briefest moment of time.

problems.why: The quoted words match Isaiah 50:2-3 (LXX), not Isaiah 44:27. LXX Isaiah 50:2 contains 'τῇ ἀβύσσῳ, ἐρημωθήσῃ, καὶ πάντας τοὺς ποταμούς σου ξηρανῶ' while 44:27 has different wording.
problems.fix: Isaiah 50:2 (or note as LXX reading differing from Hebrew)
problems.ruling: Quote 'ἐρημωθήσῃ...ξηρανῶ' matches LXX Isaiah 50:2-3, not 44:27; wrong reference misleads reader.

fixed: The quoted words match LXX Isaiah 50:2, not 44:27; corrected the citation.

problems.fix: accept with us the teaching of truth
problems.ruling: μεθ' ἡμῶν ('with us') is omitted, losing the communal appeal present in the source.

last_rejected.quote: turns it to ash through the change
last_rejected.why: ἀπαιθαλόω means to scorch/char/consume, not 'turn to ash'; lamp fire vaporizes fuel, not ash.
last_rejected.fix: quickly consumes it through the change
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπῃθάλωσε is from ἀπαιθαλόω, meaning to reduce to cinders/ash; 'turns to ash' is within normal semantic range.

last_rejected.source_quote: Ἡσαΐας ἐν οἷς πρὸς τὸν τῶν ὅλων Θεὸν διαλέγεται· Ὁ λέγων τῇ ἀβύσσῳ, ἐρημωθήσῃ, καὶ πάντας τοὺς ποταμούς σου ξηρανῶ
last_rejected.why: The quote matches Isaiah 44:27 LXX, but the source does not specify chapter/verse; the English adds a citation not in the source.
last_rejected.fix: Remove '(Isaiah 44:27)' or verify if editorial addition is permitted.
last_rejected.ruling: Isaiah 44:27 LXX matches the quote; adding the reference is standard scholarly practice, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: the finest things that are imperceptible to the senses
last_rejected.source_quote: συγκρίσει τῶν λεπτοτάτων καὶ τῇ αἰσθήσει ἀκαταλήπτων
last_rejected.why: The Greek compares the upper nature to 'the finest and imperceptible things,' not 'the finest things that are imperperceptible'—the comparison is misread as description.
last_rejected.fix: by comparison with the finest things, imperceptible to the senses
last_rejected.ruling: τῶν λεπτοτάτων καὶ τῇ αἰσθήσει ἀκαταλήπτων: 'finest things imperceptible to senses' is a reasonable rendering, not a major mistranslation.

last_rejected.why: εὐκρασία means 'good mixture/blending' or 'temperate state,' not 'temperature' in the modern sense; this is anachronistic.
last_rejected.ruling: εὐκρασία can mean 'temperate state'; 'temperature' in older sense is acceptable, not a major error.

last_rejected.why: σικύα is a cupping-glass used in medicine to draw blood/fluid; 'shows' is weak—the point is its drawing power, not demonstration.
last_rejected.ruling: σικύα as 'cupping glass' is correct; 'shows' for δηλοῖ is within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: like the fire of a lamp
last_rejected.source_quote: κατὰ τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ λυχνιαίου πυρός
last_rejected.why: εἰκών here means 'likeness/pattern' not 'like'; the lamp fire is the model or parallel case, not a simile marker.
last_rejected.fix: on the pattern of the lamp-fire
last_rejected.ruling: κατὰ εἰκόνα rendered 'like' is acceptable translation choice; 'pattern/model' is a preference, not a major error.

last_rejected.source_quote: τῷ ἀναγκαίῳ τοῦ ποιήσαντος αὐτὸν ὅρῳ
last_rejected.why: ἀναγκαῖος here means 'binding/necessary' in the sense of 'ordained by necessity,' but 'necessary limit' loses the sense of divine ordinance; 'fixed bound' or 'ordained bound' better.
last_rejected.fix: the binding bound set by its Maker
last_rejected.ruling: ἀναγκαῖον ὅρον as 'necessary limit' is within normal range; 'ordained bound' is a preference, not a major error.

last_rejected.why: ἀέριος means 'in the air' or 'of the air,' not 'aerial' in the modern sense; 'water in the air' or 'airborne water' is clearer.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀέριον as 'aerial' is within normal range; 'airborne' is a preference, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: so that the ether may not seize everything and set it on fire
last_rejected.source_quote: ὡς ἂν μὴ πάντα πυρακτῶν ὁ αἰθὴρ ἐπιλάβοι
last_rejected.why: πυρακτέω means 'to set on fire' or 'kindle,' but the construction is 'seize and set on fire'—the English splits awkwardly and 'seize everything and set it on fire' misreads πάντα as object of both verbs rather than 'all things' as comprehensive object.
last_rejected.fix: so that the ether may not seize all things and kindle them
last_rejected.ruling: πάντα as object of both ἐπιλάβοι and πυρακτῶν is a natural reading; 'seize everything and set it on fire' conveys the meaning adequately.
